```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
for (file in c("model", "complete_data", "em", "optimization", "fisher_information", "simulation", "experiments")) {
  source(file.path("..", "project_A", paste0(file, ".R")))
}
library(ggplot2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5)
```

## Algorithms and accuracy

All methods maximize the same marginal likelihood with fixed $\nu$ in $(\mu,\log v)$.
EM uses conditional latent weights and analytical maximization. BFGS uses `optim()` with the analytical
negative score. Newton solves $(-H)d=s$ and backtracks until the Armijo ascent condition holds.
If $-H$ is not positive definite, Newton uses a mean-score ascent direction; line-search failure
is reported. No method estimates $\nu$.

A fit is accuracy-certified when the maximum absolute component of the mean score, scaled by
$(\sqrt v,1)$, is at most $10^{-7}$. EM also checks relative likelihood change. BFGS must use
`optim()`'s native relative stopping rule; it is set tightly and its result must pass the same score
check. These are comparable final accuracies, not identical internal termination rules. Uncertified
fits are excluded from runtime rankings. EM likelihood monitoring is part of the measured workload.

## Repeated comparisons

Each $\nu$ uses $n=1000$, true location one, scale squared two, seed $400+\nu$, seven repetitions
and one warm-up. Within each scenario all methods use identical data and initial parameters.
Times include history collection and validation, exclude data generation and package loading, and
are machine-specific. Very short individual timings have limited resolution.

```{r}
bench <- benchmark_methods()
knitr::kable(aggregate(cbind(mu,v,loglik,seconds,objective,gradient,hessian)~nu+method,bench,median),digits=6)
knitr::kable(aggregate(converged~nu+method,bench,mean),digits=3)
knitr::kable(unique(bench[c("nu","method","iterations")]))
ggplot(bench,aes(method,seconds,color=method))+geom_point(position=position_jitter(width=.08,height=0))+
 facet_wrap(~nu,scales="free_y")+labs(title="Seven repeated optimizer timings",y="Elapsed seconds")
```

BFGS accepted iteration counts are unavailable from base `optim()` and are reported as missing.
Its function/gradient evaluations describe its effort more faithfully. EM score checks count as
gradient evaluations; the shared derivative helper also calculates a Hessian during those checks,
although no Hessian is requested by EM. Counters describe requested optimizer operations, not scalar
arithmetic. BFGS counters include rejected line-search evaluations.

```{r}
paths <- list(); summaries <- list()
for(nu in c(2,5,30)) {
 x <- simulate_t_data(1000,1,2,nu,seed=400+nu)
 fits <- fit_all(x,nu); reference <- reference_optimum(x,nu)
 stopifnot(max(sapply(fits,`[[`,"loglik"))-reference < 1e-6)
 for(method in names(fits)) {
   h <- fits[[method]]$history
   h$gap <- pmax(reference-cummax(h$loglik),1e-12)
   h$method <- method; h$nu <- nu; paths[[length(paths)+1]] <- h
 }
 summaries[[length(summaries)+1]] <- data.frame(nu,reference,
   largest_final_gap=max(reference-sapply(fits,`[[`,"loglik")))
}
paths <- do.call(rbind,paths)
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind,summaries),digits=9)
ggplot(paths,aes(iteration,gap,color=method))+geom_line()+scale_y_log10()+facet_wrap(~nu)+
 labs(title="Best objective gap along optimizer paths",x="Accepted iteration (EM/Newton); objective evaluation (BFGS)",y="Reference log-likelihood minus best attained")
ggplot(paths,aes(time,gap,color=method))+geom_line()+scale_y_log10()+
 scale_x_continuous(n.breaks=3,labels=function(z) sprintf("%.3f",z))+facet_wrap(~nu,scales="free_x")+
 labs(title="Convergence against real elapsed time",x="Elapsed seconds",y="Best objective gap")
```

The independent reference is a derivative-free Nelder–Mead optimization from three starts, using
relative tolerance $10^{-13}$. Multiple starts improve confidence but do not prove global optimality.
The curves show best-so-far likelihood and clip gaps below $10^{-12}$ for logarithmic display;
trial BFGS points need not improve the objective. Iteration axes have explicitly different meanings,
so the elapsed-time plot is the primary convergence comparison. Timing-path instrumentation itself
costs time, and these small problems should not support universal speed claims.

## Runtime distributions and convergence failures across datasets

### Paired simulation design

The seven-repeat benchmark above measures timing variation for one fixed dataset per $\nu$.
Here we also investigate variation **between datasets**: 300 independent samples of size $n=300$
for each $\nu=2,5,30$, generated at $\mu=0$, $\sigma=1$ under the correctly specified model.
These are the exact datasets used for the numerical report's Monte Carlo uncertainty study.
Every dataset is fitted with all three methods from two common starts:

- **Data-based:** $\mu_0=\operatorname{median}(x)$, $\sigma_0=\operatorname{IQR}(x)/2$.
- **Displaced:** $\mu_0=\operatorname{median}(x)+5\operatorname{IQR}(x)/2$,
  $\sigma_0=\operatorname{IQR}(x)/4$.

The displaced start is a controlled initialization challenge, not contamination: the data do not
change. It begins five initial scale units away and at half the data-based scale. For each start,
all methods receive the same dataset and parameters, tolerance $10^{-7}$, and maximum iteration
budget 200. A common iteration budget is a practical limit, not an equal amount of arithmetic:
iterations have different costs, especially when line searches are required. A failure is an
exception, a failed native stopping rule, or a result that does not meet the common score criterion.
It means an accuracy requirement was not certified within this configuration, not that the method
can never solve the problem. Passing the score check alone does not establish a global maximum.

```{r}
#| label: monte-carlo-study
#| include: false
mc <- run_monte_carlo(cache_file="results/monte_carlo.rds",source_dir="../project_A")
```

Timing starts immediately before each optimizer call and ends after its return or exception,
including validation, history collection, and internal line searches, but excluding data generation
and information-matrix calculations. An unmeasured warm-up precedes the study, and the method order
rotates across replications to reduce systematic order effects. Each dataset/start/method combination
is timed once; these distributions combine data difficulty and machine timing noise. They complement,
rather than replace, the repeated fixed-data timings above. Very short values have millisecond-scale
measurement resolution. Fits that fail still take time and are included in the distributions and
timing summaries; their speed must not be interpreted as successful optimization.

```{r}
performance <- runtime_summary(mc)
performance$scenario <- factor(performance$scenario,levels=c("Data-based","Displaced"))
performance$method <- factor(performance$method,levels=c("EM","BFGS","Newton"))
mc_fits <- mc$fits
mc_fits$scenario <- factor(mc_fits$scenario,levels=c("Data-based","Displaced"))
mc_fits$method <- factor(mc_fits$method,levels=c("EM","BFGS","Newton"))
cat(sprintf("Saved experiment completed: %s. This table covers %d timed fits.\n",mc$completed_at,nrow(mc_fits)))
performance_table <- performance[c("scenario","nu","method","fits","failures","median_ms","p90_ms")]
performance_table$failure_percent <- round(100*performance$failure_rate,1)
knitr::kable(performance_table,digits=2,row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Across-dataset performance: median and 90th-percentile elapsed milliseconds; all attempted fits included.")
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(mc_fits,aes(method,1000*seconds,fill=method))+
 geom_point(position=position_jitter(width=.14,height=0,seed=32026),
            color="grey40",alpha=.15,size=.7)+
 geom_boxplot(width=.35,outlier.shape=NA,alpha=.7)+
 geom_point(data=subset(mc_fits,!converged),shape=4,color="firebrick",size=1.5)+
 facet_grid(scenario~nu,scales="free_y")+
 labs(title="Runtime distributions across simulated datasets",
 subtitle="300 datasets per panel and method; red crosses mark uncertified fits",
 x=NULL,y="Elapsed milliseconds (includes failed fits)")+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="none")
```

The box shows the median and interquartile range; faint points show individual fits.
Points are spread horizontally only to expose ties; no artificial noise is added to elapsed times.
A smoothed density would be misleading for the many timings tied at millisecond resolution. Rows have different timing scales to make the displaced-start behavior readable; do not
compare physical heights between rows without reading the axes. Long tails indicate occasional
expensive fits that a median alone would hide. The 90th percentile in the table quantifies this
upper-runtime behavior without relying on one extreme observation.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(performance,aes(method,failure_rate,color=method))+
 geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=failure_lower,ymax=failure_upper),width=.15)+geom_point(size=2.8)+
 facet_grid(scenario~nu)+
 scale_y_continuous(labels=function(z) paste0(round(100*z,1),"%"))+
 labs(title="Convergence-failure rates under the shared accuracy check",
 subtitle="Points: observed proportions; bars: 95% Wilson intervals (300 datasets per group)",
 x=NULL,y="Uncertified fits / attempted fits")+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="none")
```

Wilson intervals remain informative when no failures occur: zero observed failures in 300 datasets
does not establish a zero underlying failure probability. The intervals describe repeated-dataset
uncertainty for each method and scenario. Because optimizers share datasets, these are paired
outcomes; overlapping or nonoverlapping marginal intervals are not a formal paired comparison.
The seeds and complete failure records are saved, so an individual problematic dataset can be
recreated rather than attributing a failed fit to the statistical model's heavy tails alone.

```{r}
for(scenario in c("Data-based","Displaced")) {
 selected <- performance[as.character(performance$scenario)==scenario,]
 cat(sprintf("From %s starts, %d of %d fits were uncertified (%.2f%%).\n",tolower(scenario),
 sum(selected$failures),sum(selected$fits),100*sum(selected$failures)/sum(selected$fits)))
 for(nu in c(2,5,30)) {
   group <- selected[selected$nu==nu,]
   cat(sprintf("At nu=%s, median runtimes span %.1f–%.1f ms and observed failure rates span %.1f–%.1f%%.\n",
   nu,min(group$median_ms),max(group$median_ms),100*min(group$failure_rate),100*max(group$failure_rate)))
 }
}
```

### Are the uncertified fits materially wrong?

A binary tolerance check can flag a nearly converged fit. To distinguish that case from a poor
solution, compare each uncertified fit with the best certified likelihood on the same dataset
(across starts). The following diagnostic reports the score residual and the likelihood gap;
it is not used to relax the success definition after seeing the results.

```{r}
certified_reference <- aggregate(loglik~nu+replication,subset(mc_fits,converged),max)
uncertified <- merge(subset(mc_fits,!converged),certified_reference,
                     by=c("nu","replication"),suffixes=c("","_reference"))
if(nrow(uncertified)>0) {
 diagnostics <- data.frame(uncertified_fits=nrow(uncertified),
   min_score_over_tolerance=min(uncertified$score,na.rm=TRUE)/mc$settings$tol,
   max_score_over_tolerance=max(uncertified$score,na.rm=TRUE)/mc$settings$tol,
   largest_loglik_gap=max(uncertified$loglik_reference-uncertified$loglik,na.rm=TRUE))
 knitr::kable(diagnostics,digits=c(0,2,2,12),row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Accuracy of uncertified fits relative to the paired certified reference.")
} else cat("No uncertified fits were observed.")
```

In this saved experiment, the uncertified results are BFGS fits that fall just short of the score
requirement. Their likelihoods are essentially indistinguishable from the paired certified fits
at the displayed statistical precision. This reflects the mismatch between `optim()`'s native
relative-objective stopping rule and our post-fit score certification, rather than evidence that
BFGS has found statistically different estimates. A tighter or differently controlled termination
procedure could change these rates. We retain the predefined rule and report both the binary
outcome and its numerical size rather than changing settings to hide failures.

A fast optimizer that misses the requested tolerance is not a substitute for a slower certified
fit. Read the runtime and failure plots together. The common score check makes reported successes
comparable even though BFGS uses its native stopping rule internally. The study does not tune starts,
iteration limits or tolerances separately to favor an optimizer. Its results are conditional on
the chosen sample size, start rules, and implementation instrumentation, and do not imply universal
rankings. In particular, changing optimization methods should not change the MLE's sampling uncertainty
when they reach the same maximum; the numerical report verifies this with paired estimate spreads.

The raw experiment is shared through `report/results/monte_carlo.rds`. It is reused across report
renders when settings and R sources match. The saved timestamp identifies when the timings were
actually measured. Delete the file or use `force=TRUE` in `run_monte_carlo()` for fresh measurements;
data seeds remain reproducible, while runtime distributions naturally vary.

## Does contamination change optimizer performance?

### Controlled design

This replaces the one-outlier robustness illustration with a **paired algorithm comparison**.
The numerical report explains the model's weighting mechanism and checks agreement of certified
estimates. Here the outcomes are runtime, convergence success and numerical accuracy.

There are 100 independent $t_5$ baseline datasets ($n=500$, location 0, scale 1; seed $47000+b$).
Each baseline supplies three samples with exactly 0%, 1% or 5% of its observations replaced by
independent $N(15,1)$ values. The randomly selected positions and outlier values are nested across
levels. Each sample is fitted with fixed $\nu=2,5,30$ using every optimizer and two common starts:

- **Data-based:** sample median and half-IQR scale.
- **Displaced:** that location plus five initial scale units, with half the initial scale.

Starts are recomputed for each contaminated sample and are identical across optimizers and fixed
$\nu$ values. Thus the study measures the full effect of contamination, including on initialization.
All data and starts are paired between methods. The displaced start changes initialization while
holding the sample fixed. Contamination changes the data; it is not a different optimizer or a
change in fitted $\nu$. The fitted tail assumptions differ while the baseline generating model
remains $t_5$. We study only one-sided distant contamination, so other outlier mechanisms may behave differently.

We keep the same accuracy check $10^{-7}$ and maximum iteration budget 200 for every method.
Iteration limits are not equal-work budgets: line searches and curvature computations differ.
Each dataset/level/nu/start/method fit is timed once, after an unmeasured warm-up, with method order
rotated across replications. Timings include validation, trace collection and unsuccessful fits,
and exclude data generation and summary calculations. These are workload distributions across
100 datasets, not 100 repetitions of one fixed input. There are **5,400 timed fits** in this study.

```{r}
#| label: contamination-study
#| include: false
contamination <- run_contamination_study(cache_file="results/contamination.rds",source_dir="../project_A")
contamination_performance <- contamination_summary(contamination)
contamination_checks <- contamination_agreement(contamination)
```

```{r}
cp <- contamination_performance
cp$method <- factor(cp$method,levels=c("EM","BFGS","Newton"))
cp$scenario <- factor(cp$scenario,levels=c("Data-based","Displaced"))
cf <- contamination$fits
cf$method <- factor(cf$method,levels=c("EM","BFGS","Newton"))
cf$scenario <- factor(cf$scenario,levels=c("Data-based","Displaced"))
cf$percent <- 100*cf$fraction
compact <- cp[c("scenario","nu","percent","method")]
compact$entry <- sprintf("%.1f / %.1f / %d",cp$median_ms,cp$p90_ms,cp$failures)
compact <- reshape(compact,idvar=c("scenario","nu","percent"),timevar="method",direction="wide")
names(compact) <- sub("entry\\.","",names(compact))
compact <- compact[order(compact$scenario,compact$nu,compact$percent),]
knitr::kable(compact,row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Each method cell: median ms / 90th-percentile ms / uncertified fits out of 100. Failed fits remain in timing summaries.")
cat(sprintf("Timings were measured in the saved run completed %s.\n",contamination$completed_at))
```

### Runtime distributions

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(cf,aes(factor(percent),1000*seconds,fill=method))+
 geom_boxplot(position=position_dodge(.75),width=.65,outlier.size=.7,alpha=.7)+
 facet_grid(scenario~nu,scales="free_y")+
 labs(title="Optimizer runtime as contamination increases",
 subtitle="100 paired datasets per level; all attempts included",
 x="Contaminated observations (%)",y="Elapsed milliseconds",fill="Optimizer")+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

Each box describes one optimizer at a contamination level: the center is the median, the box spans
the interquartile range, and points beyond the whiskers expose unusually expensive fits. Rows have
separate y-scales, so compare their numerical axes rather than physical box heights. Methods share
datasets, and contamination levels share baselines. A consistently shifted distribution is more
informative than a single unusually fast or slow fit. Millisecond resolution and timing instrumentation
limit conclusions about very small differences. A fast failed fit is not an accurate MLE.

### Convergence success

A fit is uncertified if an exception occurs, its native convergence test fails, or its final mean
score exceeds the shared dimensionless tolerance. We do not silently exclude it or redefine the
criterion after seeing the data. The following plot shows failure proportions with 95% Wilson
intervals. Zero failures out of 100 still allows an underlying probability of roughly 3.7% at the
upper Wilson bound; it is not proof of perfect reliability. These intervals are marginal uncertainty
summaries, not a formal test of paired differences between optimizers.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6.5
ggplot(cp,aes(factor(percent),failure_rate,color=method,group=method))+
 geom_line(position=position_dodge(.35))+
 geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=failure_lower,ymax=failure_upper),position=position_dodge(.35),width=.1)+
 geom_point(position=position_dodge(.35),size=2.2)+facet_grid(scenario~nu)+
 scale_y_continuous(labels=function(z) paste0(round(100*z),"%"))+
 labs(title="Does contamination make convergence less reliable?",
 subtitle="Uncertified fits under the same score tolerance; bars are 95% Wilson intervals",
 x="Contaminated observations (%)",y="Uncertified attempts",color="Optimizer")+
 theme_minimal(base_size=12)+theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

### Final likelihood agreement and size of tolerance misses

We compare certified solutions only within the **same dataset, contamination level and fixed $\nu$**.
The reference is the largest certified likelihood across methods and both starts. It is a best-attained
reference, not a proven global optimum; it suffices for an agreement check. The numerical report shows
the distribution of certified likelihood spreads. Here we also inspect uncertified outputs: a score
just above $10^{-7}$ is a different issue from a materially worse likelihood.

```{r}
checks <- contamination_checks
max_or_na <- function(x) if(all(is.na(x))) NA_real_ else max(x,na.rm=TRUE)
accuracy_table <- do.call(rbind,lapply(split(checks,interaction(checks[c("nu","percent")],drop=TRUE)),function(g) {
 data.frame(nu=g$nu[1],percent=g$percent[1],datasets_without_certified_fit=sum(g$certified==0),
 max_certified_loglik_spread=max_or_na(g$loglik_spread),
 largest_uncertified_loglik_gap=max_or_na(g$uncertified_gap),
 largest_uncertified_score=max_or_na(g$uncertified_score))
}))
accuracy_table <- accuracy_table[order(accuracy_table$nu,accuracy_table$percent),]
for(column in c("max_certified_loglik_spread","largest_uncertified_loglik_gap","largest_uncertified_score"))
 accuracy_table[[column]] <- ifelse(is.na(accuracy_table[[column]]),"NA",formatC(accuracy_table[[column]],format="e",digits=2))
knitr::kable(accuracy_table,row.names=FALSE,
 caption="Numerical agreement and tolerance misses; NA means no uncertified finite-likelihood output in that cell.")
```

Small gaps show that a binary failure rate can exaggerate practical differences in the estimates.
Large gaps, if present, would instead warrant investigation of initialization, curvature, or local
solutions. A failed fit remains failed under the declared rule in either case. The error records,
seeds, starting parameters and score residuals are retained in the RDS file for diagnosis.

```{r}
for(scenario in c("Data-based","Displaced")) {
 for(method in c("EM","BFGS","Newton")) {
  selected <- cp[as.character(cp$scenario)==scenario & as.character(cp$method)==method,]
  cat(sprintf("%s / %s: %d uncertified fits out of %d attempts across the three contamination levels and fitted nu values.\n",
  scenario,method,sum(selected$failures),sum(selected$fits)))
 }
}
cat(sprintf("Largest likelihood spread among certified fits: %.3g.\n",max(checks$loglik_spread,na.rm=TRUE)))
for(method in c("EM","BFGS","Newton")) {
 selected <- cp[cp$nu==30 & as.character(cp$scenario)=="Displaced" & as.character(cp$method)==method,]
 cat(sprintf("For nu=30 from displaced starts, %s median runtime changed from %.1f ms at 0%% contamination to %.1f ms at 5%%.\n",
 method,selected$median_ms[selected$percent==0],selected$median_ms[selected$percent==5]))
}
cat(sprintf("Among uncertified finite-likelihood results, the largest gap from a paired certified reference is %.3g; the largest score residual is %.2f times the prescribed tolerance.\n",
 max(checks$uncertified_gap,na.rm=TRUE),max(checks$uncertified_score,na.rm=TRUE)/contamination$settings$tol))

```

In this run, all EM and Newton attempts were certified; the uncertified BFGS outcomes were
near-tolerance misses with almost identical likelihoods, rather than substantially different solutions.
Nevertheless, the displaced-start runtime comparison at $\nu=30$ reveals that contamination can
increase computational effort even when the final estimates agree. The runtime changes differ
between optimizers, so model robustness alone does not predict optimization speed.

Read the runtime and failure plots together. Contamination need not slow every method monotonically:
it changes curvature, relative weights, data-based starts and native stopping behavior. Any observed
trend is conditional on this contamination mechanism and these implementations. The experiment
compares the cost of reaching a common likelihood solution, not different statistical robustness
for different optimizers. The statistical response to outliers depends on the fitted $\nu$.

The saved `report/results/contamination.rds` is shared by both reports and contains the raw paired
results. Delete it or call `run_contamination_study(..., force=TRUE)` for fresh timings. Code or
setting changes invalidate the cache. Its saved timestamp identifies the actual measurement run.

## Profiling and a targeted improvement

We profile 25 readable EM fits on $n=20000$ observations from $t_2$ (seed 188), sampling every
2 ms. Profiling is statistical: sampled proportions vary across runs. The following table contains
actual inclusive and self times, not predicted bottlenecks.

```{r}
profile <- profile_em()
relevant <- profile$profile$by.total
relevant <- relevant[grepl("fit_em|em_step|complete_data|joint_logdensity|conditional_weights|t_loglik|t_derivatives|score_error|validate_model", rownames(relevant)), , drop=FALSE]
knitr::kable(relevant)
knitr::kable(head(profile$profile$by.self,8))
cat(sprintf("Total sampled time: %.3f seconds.",profile$profile$sampling.time))
```

The self-time table shows that instrumentation (`proc.time`) can itself dominate this small
profiled workload. Marginal density evaluations (`dt`) and derivative calculations also contribute;
therefore the profile describes the monitored implementation, rather than just mathematical EM
updates. Repeated vector allocations are visible indirectly in these R operations; this profile
does not measure allocation volume. Removing all timing would prevent the requested real-time
convergence curves, so the same timing policy is retained for the comparison.

The readable M-step calls `complete_data_mle()`, which validates by evaluating the complete joint
density. EM only needs weighted sums once its data and weights are valid. The optional `optimized=TRUE`
branch eliminates that unused density evaluation and uses the same weighted formulas. This is a
small duplication kept next to the original update to make the measured change easy to inspect.
The following repeated timings determine whether it helps on this workload; no C++ is required to
remove unused work. Other entries, such as marginal density evaluation and derivative calculations,
remain candidates for future work rather than unmeasured speedup claims.

```{r}
comparison <- profile$comparison
stopifnot(max(abs(comparison$mu-comparison$mu[1]))<1e-12,
          max(abs(comparison$v-comparison$v[1]))<1e-12,
          max(abs(comparison$loglik-comparison$loglik[1]))<1e-9,
          all(comparison$converged))
knitr::kable(aggregate(seconds~optimized,comparison,median),digits=5)
speedup <- median(comparison$seconds[!comparison$optimized])/median(comparison$seconds[comparison$optimized])
cat(sprintf("Measured median speed ratio (readable / streamlined): %.2f. No compilation time is involved.",speedup))
```

## Conclusions supported by this run

```{r}
for(nu in c(2,5,30)) {
 selected <- bench[bench$nu==nu & bench$converged,]
 timing <- aggregate(seconds~method,selected,median)
 winner <- timing$method[which.min(timing$seconds)]
 cat(sprintf("For nu = %s, %s has the smallest median time among certified fits. ",nu,winner))
}
cat(sprintf("Across all recorded benchmark fits, %d of %d passed the common accuracy check.",sum(bench$converged),nrow(bench)))
```

EM's update is easy to derive and monotone; Newton requires more derivative and line-search code;
BFGS relies on a standard optimizer and supplies intermediate effort through evaluation counts.
The measured winners apply to these sample sizes, starts and implementations. EM iteration counts
alone cannot establish efficiency. Statistical robustness is controlled by $\nu$; computational cost
is controlled by the optimizer and its implementation. Tests validate the density, EM updates,
derivatives and information before these performance experiments.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
sessionInfo()
```
